title: Anchored Decoding: Provably Reducing Copyright Risk for Any Language Model
claim: Constraining a risky model to stay near a safe one avoids verbatim copying while keeping near-original utility, beating prior methods.
layout: 2 panels: left worked example diagram, right stacked Pareto plots with 'ours' highlighted
description: Two panels. Panel (a) on the left is an example generation. An input prompt (a Bilbo Baggins line from Tolkien) sits at the top and has arrows going down to a risky LM (pink network, p_r) on the left and a safe LM (teal network, p_s) on the right. Both feed logits into a central purple-titled 'Anchored Decoding' box. The box states the goal as a KL budget, gives the constrained argmin objective, and shows a small geometric sketch: a cyan ball around p_s with radius k_t, and the projected distribution p_t* on its boundary. Below are three text boxes: the risky LM output, flagged 'Copyrighted text!'; the safe LM output, flagged 'Lower quality!'; and the Anchored Decoding output at the bottom. Panel (b) on the right has two stacked plots, Fluency and Factuality, against normalized copying reduction (%). The purple 'ours' curve stays high and flat until about 100%, while the baselines drop off. A shaded region marks reduction above 75%.
caption: (a). Given the opening line of J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Fellowship of the Ring (1954), the risky LM outputs its verbatim continuation, while the safe LM produces a less fluent, repetitive alternative. ANCHORED DECODING generates in bounded proximity to the safe LM within a budget K, while leveraging utility from the risky LM, and produces a plausible, non-infringing continuation. (b). With the safe-risky LM pair {TinyComma 1.8B, Llama 3.1 70B}, ANCHORED DECODING (in purple) achieves the best risk-utility tradeoff.
abstract: Language models (LMs) tend to memorize portions of their training data and emit verbatim spans. When the underlying sources are sensitive or copyright-protected, such reproduction raises issues of consent and compensation for creators and compliance risks for developers. We propose Anchored Decoding, a plug-and-play inference-time method for suppressing verbatim copying: it enables decoding from any risky LM trained on mixed-license data by keeping generation in bounded proximity to a permissively trained safe LM. Anchored Decoding adaptively allocates a user-chosen information budget over the generation trajectory and enforces per-step constraints that yield a sequence-level guarantee, enabling a tunable risk-utility trade-off. To make Anchored Decoding practically useful, we introduce a new permissively trained safe model (TinyComma 1.8B), as well as Anchored$_{\mathrm{Byte}}$ Decoding, a byte-level variant of our method that enables cross-vocabulary fusion via the ByteSampler framework (Hayase et al., 2025). Across six model pairs on long-form metrics for copying risk and utility, Anchored and Anchored$_{\mathrm{Byte}}$ Decoding define a new Pareto frontier, preserving near-original fluency and factuality while closing up to 75% of the measurable copying gap between the risky baseline and a safe reference, at a modest inference overhead.
